approach: Test the claim with free fall from rest: at the starting instant velocity is zero, but the acceleration a = v dv/ds still gives a finite, nonzero value.

steps.text: For free fall from rest through a height s, the speed follows v² = 2gs, so v = √(2gs) and dv/ds = g/v.
Form the product a = v dv/ds; the v in front cancels the v in the denominator of dv/ds, leaving a constant, even as v approaches zero near the start.
steps.why_this_step: As s becomes very small, v also becomes very small, but dv/ds grows without bound, so the product v dv/ds stays finite and equal to g rather than going to zero.

steps.text: This shows a = v dv/ds does not force acceleration to zero when velocity is zero; the Assertion's conclusion is false, while the Reason, that a in this formula is the instantaneous acceleration, is a true definition on its own and does not justify the false conclusion.

final_answer.value: If Assertion is false but the Reason is true.

common_mistakes.text: Substituting v = 0 directly into a = v dv/ds and reading off a = 0, without checking that dv/ds can be infinite at that point.
